what: A workflow engine runs long, multi-step jobs and remembers where each one is. If a server crashes mid-way, the job resumes from the last finished step instead of starting over.
like: Like a recipe card where you tick each step as you go: if the phone rings, you come back and carry on from the last tick, not from scratch.
why: Long jobs (minutes to months) survive crashes, deploys and restarts
Retries, timeouts and waits are handled for you, not hand-written each time
Every step is recorded, so you can see exactly where a run is and why it failed

nodes.t: Retry policy|1 s, x2, up to 100 s

steps.d: Your API asks the engine to start, say, 'research company X'. The engine gives it an ID and records a start event.
A worker runs your workflow function. It must be deterministic (same input, same decisions), so it never reads the clock or calls APIs directly.
LLM calls, web searches and database writes run as activities. Each result is saved in the event history before the next step starts.
A failed activity retries with backoff: Temporal's default starts at 1 s, doubles each time, caps at 100 s and keeps trying unless you set limits.
A new worker replays the event history. Finished activities return their recorded results instead of running again, so the run continues from where it stopped.
Timers and signals let a run pause for a human approval. The worker goes idle while the server holds the state, for seconds or months.

choices.d: Temporal for code-first durable workflows; Step Functions for AWS-native JSON state machines; Airflow for scheduled batch DAGs; LangGraph for agent graphs with checkpoints.
Set a start-to-close timeout per activity and a retry policy. Mark permanent errors (bad input) as non-retryable so they fail fast instead of retrying forever.
One activity per side effect (one LLM call, one write). Smaller steps mean less rework after a crash, but every step adds history events.
Loops and agents that run for weeks grow history. Use Continue-As-New in Temporal, or start a fresh execution in Step Functions, before hitting the limits.
For LangGraph, pick a checkpointer: SqliteSaver for local work, PostgresSaver for production, keyed by thread_id so each conversation resumes correctly.

instead.why: Fine for single-step jobs; you hand-build retries and state
Scheduled data pipelines rather than per-request long-running jobs
A simple in-memory agent loop for short tasks
The approval step itself, which a workflow engine can host

breaks.d: Workflow code used the system clock, random numbers or changed step order in a deploy.
breaks.see: Replay fails with a non-deterministic error and the run is stuck
breaks.fix: Use SDK time and random APIs, move I/O into activities, version code changes

breaks.d: An agent loop adds events every turn until it reaches the limit.
breaks.see: History size warnings at 10,240 events, then the hard limit stops the run
breaks.fix: Continue-As-New with a small state summary

breaks.d: A worker finished the work but crashed before reporting, so it is retried.
breaks.see: Duplicate emails, double writes or two charges
breaks.fix: Idempotent activities with an idempotency key or upserts

breaks.d: Whole documents or LLM outputs are passed between steps.
breaks.see: Payload size errors, slow history loading
breaks.fix: Store blobs in object storage and pass only the key

breaks.d: Default activity retries are unlimited, so a permanent error keeps retrying.
breaks.see: Runs stay open for days with the same error each attempt
breaks.fix: Non-retryable error types, maximum attempts or a schedule-to-close timeout

say: For long multi-step AI jobs I'd use a durable workflow engine like Temporal: the workflow code decides the steps and every LLM or search call is an activity with its own timeout and retry policy.
The engine records each step in an event history, so if a worker dies it replays the history and carries on without repeating finished work.
Activities are idempotent with a job key, because at-least-once retries mean any one of them can run twice.
For human review the workflow waits on a signal with a timer as a deadline, which costs nothing while it waits.

followups.q: Why must workflow code be deterministic?
followups.a: Recovery works by replaying the history and re-running the code. If the code makes different decisions on replay, say from reading the clock, its commands no longer match the history and the engine raises a non-determinism error.

Airflow schedules batch DAGs of data tasks, usually on a timetable. Temporal runs many per-request workflows written as normal code, with signals, long waits and fine-grained retries. Many teams use both.

A LangGraph checkpointer saves the graph state per thread_id, which enables human-in-the-loop pauses, time travel and recovery for agents. Temporal adds durable retries, timers and signals around a whole multi-step job.

followups.q: How do you handle an agent that runs for weeks?
followups.a: Keep each turn as activities, summarise state, and call Continue-As-New before the history nears the event limit. Large tool outputs go to storage, with only keys in the history.

check.q: Where should an LLM API call go in a Temporal workflow?
check.why: Workflow code must be deterministic; activities do the real I/O and get retries.

check.q: A worker crashes halfway through a run. What happens?
check.a: Another worker replays the history and continues
d: The whole run starts from step one
A human must restart it by hand
check.why: Finished activities return their recorded results during replay.

check.q: Your agent loop has run 10,000 turns. What should it do?
check.why: History has a hard event limit, and starting a fresh run resets it.

check.a: Retries mean an activity can run more than once
check.why: A crash after doing the work but before reporting causes a retry.
